title: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHO WAS HE PRAYING TO? THE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT CHRIST
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHO WAS HE PRAYING TO? THE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT CHRIST

Jesus said, “I and my Father are one.” Yet He lifted His eyes toward heaven and prayed. Was He talking to Himself? Was He less than God? Or does this moment reveal something so extraordinary about the Father, the Son, and the love that carried Jesus to the cross that we cannot afford to misunderstand it?
There is a question that has troubled sincere believers, confused new Christians, and given skeptics something to challenge for centuries.
And perhaps, somewhere deep inside, you have wondered about it too.
If Jesus is God, why did He pray to God?
Think about that for a moment.
Jesus commanded storms to be still, and the winds obeyed Him.
He called Lazarus out of a tomb, and a dead man walked into the daylight.
He forgave sins, received worship, and declared that before Abraham existed, He already was.
Then, on another occasion, this same Jesus looked toward heaven and began speaking to His Father.
Not performing for a crowd.
Not pretending to pray.
Actually praying.
And suddenly, the question becomes impossible to ignore.
If Jesus and the Father are one, why would Jesus need to speak to the Father at all?
Was He talking to Himself?
Was He somehow less than the One He called Father?
Did His prayers prove He was not truly God?
Or have we misunderstood what Jesus meant when He said they were one?
Because here is what makes this question so important.
If we misunderstand who Jesus is, we risk misunderstanding the very One who came to save us.
And the answer is not found by avoiding the difficult verses.
It is found by opening them.
By listening carefully.
By allowing Scripture to explain Scripture.
And by discovering that the prayers of Jesus do not weaken His divine identity.
They reveal something breathtaking about it.
In John 10:30, Jesus makes one of the most astonishing declarations recorded in the Gospels:
“I and my Father are one.” — John 10:30, KJV
The original Greek reads:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho patēr hen esmen.
Literally:
“I and the Father are one.”
Now look carefully at two words.
ἕν — hen.
ἐσμεν — esmen.
The word hen means “one.” It is grammatically neuter, rather than the masculine form that would more naturally suggest one individual person.
And esmen means “we are.”
Not “I am.”
“We are.”
That distinction matters.
Jesus did not say that He and the Father were the same person.
He spoke of Himself and the Father distinctly while declaring their oneness.
The grammar alone does not explain the entire doctrine of the Trinity. But it fits the distinction Scripture repeatedly makes between the Father and the Son.
They are not one person wearing different masks.
Nor are they two competing gods.
The historic Christian confession is that the Father and the Son are distinct persons who share the one undivided divine being.
And the immediate context makes it clear that Jesus was claiming something extraordinary.
The people listening understood that His words carried tremendous weight.
John 10:33 records their accusation:
“Thou, being a man, makest thyself God.” — KJV
They picked up stones.
Why?
Because they believed He was making a blasphemous claim.
Jesus did not respond by saying that He was merely a religious teacher who had been misunderstood.
Instead, He continued speaking of His unique relationship with the Father, saying in John 10:38 that the Father was in Him and He in the Father.
But now we arrive at the question that changes the entire conversation.
If Jesus truly shared the divine nature, why do we find Him praying?
To understand that, we need to enter one of the most sacred moments in the Gospel of John.
Not the scene where Jesus silenced a storm.
Not the scene where He multiplied bread.
Not even the scene where Lazarus emerged from his grave.
We need to stand, in our imagination, near Jesus as the shadow of the cross draws closer.
His betrayal is approaching.
His disciples are about to be scattered.
The suffering of Calvary is near.
And Jesus lifts His eyes toward heaven.
John 17:1 records:
“Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee.” — KJV
Stop there.
Read it again.
“Father, the hour is come.”
He knows what is coming.
He knows the betrayal.
The rejection.
The humiliation.
The nails.
The cross.
And instead of running from the Father's purpose, He prays.
This is not a confused man desperately trying to discover His identity.
This is the eternal Son, having taken on genuine human nature, speaking to the Father with whom He has eternally shared divine glory.
And what He says next is astonishing.
In John 17:5, Jesus prays:
“And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.” — KJV
Before the world was.
Before Bethlehem.
Before Abraham.
Before Adam drew his first breath.
Before there was a mountain, an ocean, a star, or a human heartbeat.
Jesus speaks of glory He already possessed with the Father.
The Greek expression is especially significant:
πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι
Pro tou ton kosmon einai.
“Before the world existed.”
Jesus was not merely asking to become glorious for the first time.
He was speaking of glory He had with the Father before creation.
And notice the relational language.
“With thee.”
With the Father.
Not simply as the Father.
With the Father.
This is where the answer begins to unfold.
Jesus prayed to the Father because the Son is not the Father.
And Jesus could pray as a man because the eternal Son had truly become human.
Two truths.
Both essential.
Neither can be discarded without distorting the biblical picture.
Christianity does not teach that Jesus is the Father.
It teaches that Jesus is God the Son.
The Father is God.
The Son is God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
Yet there are not three gods, but one God.
The Father is not the Son. The Son is not the Spirit. The Spirit is not the Father.
The three persons are distinct, yet share the one divine essence.
This is what Christians mean by the Trinity.
Not three separate divine beings.
Not one person changing costumes.
One God, eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
And while the word Trinity is not written in the Bible, the doctrine seeks to faithfully express the truths Scripture reveals together.
The opening of John's Gospel gives us a remarkable foundation.
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — John 1:1, KJV
In Greek:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos.
The Word was with God.
And the Word was God.
John holds both truths together.
Personal distinction.
Full deity.

The Greek expression pros ton theon speaks of the Word being with God, while theos ēn ho logos affirms the divine identity of the Word. The grammar does not mean that the Word was merely one lesser god among others.
Then John 1:14 tells us:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” — KJV
That is the miracle of the incarnation.
The eternal Son did not stop being God.
He became truly human.
He did not exchange divinity for humanity.
He took humanity to Himself.
And this matters more than we often realize.
Because when Jesus prayed, He was not demonstrating that He lacked deity.
He was living a genuinely human life of communion, obedience, and dependence upon His Father.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ as existing in the form of God, yet humbling Himself, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death.
The Greek of Philippians 2:7 includes the words:
μορφὴν δούλου λαβών
Morphēn doulou labōn.
“Taking the form of a servant.”
Notice the word taking.
The Son's humility involved taking the servant's condition, not ceasing to possess the divine nature.
Jesus became what He had not previously been—truly human—without ceasing to be who He eternally is.
The historic Christian understanding is that Jesus Christ is one person with two natures: fully God and fully man.
Not half God and half man.
Not a divine person temporarily pretending to be human.
Not an ordinary man who later earned divine status.
The eternal Son truly entered our humanity.
And that means His human life was real.
His hunger was real.
His exhaustion was real.
His tears were real.
His suffering was real.
His prayers were real.
When Jesus prayed, He was not staging a conversation for an audience.
The Son was genuinely addressing the Father.
And as the incarnate Son, He lived the perfect human obedience that we have failed to live.
Think about what that means for your own life.
Have you ever been so exhausted that you could barely form a prayer?
Have you ever knelt beside your bed, trying to find words, while everything inside you felt heavy?
Have you ever whispered, “Father, I don't know what to do anymore”?
Jesus knows what it means to pray in human weakness.
Not because He was sinful.
He was without sin.
But because He truly entered the conditions of our human existence, including suffering, sorrow, and temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
And Hebrews 5:7 describes Him offering prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears.
The One who created the human voice used a human voice to pray.
The One who sustains creation entered a human life in which He experienced weariness and suffering.
The One who knew the glory of heaven willingly walked the road to Calvary.
Not because He had lost His divine identity.
But because He came to save people who could never save themselves.
And perhaps that is where this question stops being merely theological.
Because behind the question, “Why did Jesus pray?” is another question.
Why would the eternal Son willingly come this close to our brokenness?
Why enter a world filled with betrayal?
Why experience rejection?
Why accept humiliation?
Why submit to death on a cross?
Scripture gives us the answer.
Love.
Not sentimental love that ignores evil.
Not shallow love that pretends sin does not matter.
Holy love.
Sacrificial love.
Redeeming love.
The kind of love that confronts our rebellion while opening the way for our forgiveness.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Not after we convinced everyone that we were spiritually strong.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And suddenly, the prayer of Jesus in John 17 becomes even more beautiful.
He is not merely speaking about glory.
He is approaching the hour through which the Father's saving purpose will be accomplished.
John 17:4 records Jesus saying:
“I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.” — KJV
These words anticipate the completion of His earthly mission, which will reach its climax in His death and resurrection.
And later, from the cross, Jesus will cry:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30, KJV
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
The word communicates completion.
In its immediate Gospel context, Jesus is declaring the fulfillment of the work leading to His death, not offering a vague promise that earthly suffering has ended for everyone who believes.
His sacrifice was not an accident.
The cross was not God's emergency response to a failed plan.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
John 10:18 makes that clear.
And this is why we must never separate the identity of Jesus from the mission of Jesus.
If He were merely another religious teacher, His death could inspire us, but it could not accomplish what the New Testament says His sacrifice accomplished.
If He were not truly human, He would not have entered our condition as the representative and mediator of His people.
But Scripture presents Him as the incarnate Son, fully divine and fully human, the one mediator between God and humanity.
First Timothy 2:5 says:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — KJV
The same Jesus who shares divine glory with the Father is the mediator who gave Himself for us.
This is not a contradiction.
It is the wonder of the incarnation.
And now consider another objection.
Someone may say, “But Jesus said the Father is greater than He is.”
Yes.
John 14:28 records those words.
We should never hide them.
We should understand them alongside the rest of Scripture.
Jesus was speaking as the Son who had entered the humble condition of the incarnation and was returning to the Father.
His submission in His earthly mission does not require us to conclude that He possesses an inferior divine nature.
Philippians 2 explains His willing humiliation.
John 17:5 reveals His glory with the Father before the world existed.
And John 5:23 teaches that the Son is to be honored just as the Father is honored.
We cannot faithfully interpret one verse by silencing the others.
Someone else may ask, “But if Jesus is God, how could He say that He did not know the day or hour?”
Mark 13:32 does indeed record Jesus saying that the Son did not know the day or hour.
That verse deserves careful attention, not dismissal.
The incarnation is not an illusion. Jesus possessed a genuine human mind and underwent genuine human development, as Luke 2:52 describes.
Christian theologians have explained the relationship between Christ's divine knowledge and His human knowledge in different ways. The precise mechanics remain mysterious.
But the New Testament does not treat His real human limitations as proof that the eternal Word was not divine.
It presents the incarnate Christ as truly human while also affirming His divine identity.
We must be humble enough to acknowledge what Scripture reveals without pretending to explain every mystery beyond it.
And perhaps the most emotionally difficult objection comes from the cross itself.
When Jesus cried:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” — Matthew 27:46, KJV
Was the Trinity broken?
Did the Son cease to be God?
Did the Father stop loving the Son?
No.
Jesus was quoting the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins with the anguish of apparent abandonment and moves toward vindication and praise.
His cry expressed the real horror of His suffering.
The New Testament also teaches that Christ bore our sins and endured the judgment associated with them.
Yet Scripture does not teach that the divine nature was torn apart or that the eternal Trinity ceased to exist.
The Son's suffering was real.
His sacrifice was real.
His cry was real.
But God's eternal being was not shattered at Calvary.
The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did not become enemies or separate gods.
The cross reveals the terrible seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of God's saving love.
And this brings us back to John 17.
Because there is something in that chapter that many people overlook.
Jesus did not pray only about Himself.
He prayed for His disciples.
And then He prayed for those who would believe through their message.
That includes believers who came centuries later.
John 17:20 records:
“Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word.” — KJV
Think about that.
Before the nails.
Before the crown of thorns.
Before the darkness of Calvary.
Jesus prayed for those who would come to believe in Him.
For the church that would be formed through the apostolic witness.
For people who had not yet been born.
For believers who would struggle.
For disciples who would stumble.
For Christians who would need grace every single day.
And if you belong to Christ, this prayer concerns you.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret battle.
Maybe your family sees someone strong, but your private life tells another story.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine,” while your heart is quietly falling apart.
Maybe you have spent years attending church while struggling to believe that God could still welcome someone with your history.
Or maybe you have never truly surrendered to Jesus at all.
You know the language.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
But somewhere between religious activity and daily life, your heart has grown distant.
And now you are wondering whether there is still a way back.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not that your sins are insignificant.
They are not.
The answer is not that repentance is unnecessary.
It is necessary.
The answer is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
He does not invite you to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
He calls you to turn from it and trust Him.
He offers forgiveness and a new life grounded in His death and resurrection.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Not because sin has become harmless.
But because Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
This is the Gospel.
This is the grace that confronts scandal.
This is the redemption that reaches into ruined stories.
And this is why the words “From Scandal to Grace” are more than a memorable phrase.
They describe the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
The person who lied can repent and learn to walk in truth.
The person who betrayed trust can confess, seek reconciliation, and begin the difficult work of rebuilding what was damaged.
The person trapped in bitterness can learn forgiveness.
The person ashamed of yesterday can discover that yesterday does not have to govern tomorrow.
Not every earthly consequence disappears.
Not every relationship is instantly restored.
Not every wound heals overnight.
But in Christ, guilt does not have to be the final word.
Sin does not have to remain your master.
And your past does not have to become your identity.
Because Jesus does not merely improve the appearance of a broken life.
He reconciles sinners to God and begins transforming them from the inside out.
Now return to the original question.
If Jesus and the Father are one, why did Jesus pray to the Father?
Because their oneness is not the erasure of their personal distinction.
Because the eternal Son truly became human.
Because His prayers expressed genuine communion with His Father and perfect obedience in His earthly mission.
Because He came not merely to teach us about prayer, but to accomplish our salvation.
And because the Father and the Son have never been two rival gods struggling for control.
Jesus was not talking to Himself.
He was speaking to His Father.
The Son who was with the Father before creation had entered human history to fulfill the Father's saving purpose.
And His prayers reveal both the reality of His humanity and the eternal relationship that the incarnation did not destroy.
This is not something we should reduce to a clever argument for winning debates.
It is truth that should lead us toward worship.
Because the One who prayed in John 17 is the same One who went to the cross.
The same One who rose from the dead.
The same One whom Scripture presents as our risen Lord and intercessor.
Romans 8:34 declares that Christ is risen, is at the right hand of God, and makes intercession for us.
Hebrews 7:25 teaches that He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
Consider the comfort in that.
Your salvation does not rest on your ability to produce perfect prayers.
It rests on the finished work and continuing priestly ministry of Jesus Christ.
When you cannot find the words, He has not stopped being your Savior.
When you are confronted by your sin, His grace does not become permission to hide.
It becomes the reason to come into the light.
When you stumble, you do not need to pretend you never fell.
You need to return to Christ in repentance and faith.
And when someone tells you that Jesus cannot be God because He prayed, you do not need to panic.
Open John 10.
Open John 17.
Open John 1.
Read Philippians 2.
Read Hebrews.
Let the whole witness of Scripture speak.
The same Bible that records Jesus praying also declares His eternal glory.
The same Bible that reveals His obedience also reveals His divine identity.
The same Bible that describes His tears also tells us that all things were made through Him.
And the same Bible that takes us to His cross leads us to His empty tomb.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy would be to spend our lives arguing about whether Jesus could pray while never personally responding to the One who came to save us.
Because this question is not merely asking what you think about Jesus.
Eventually, it confronts you with what you will do with Him.
Will you keep Him at a safe intellectual distance?
Will you admire His teachings while refusing His lordship?
Will you continue hiding behind religious familiarity?
Or will you surrender?
Not to an institution.
Not to a personality.
Not to a ministry.
To Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The eternal Son who became man.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
If this truth has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
You can begin with a simple, sincere prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I believe You are the Son of God who came in the flesh, died for sinners, and rose again. I confess that I have sinned against You. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from what dishonors You. Help me trust Your Word, follow Your truth, and live for Your glory. I do not want merely to know facts about You. I want to know You, obey You, and belong to You. Amen.”

The words themselves are not a magic formula. Salvation is not earned by repeating a prayer. It is God's gracious gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ, and genuine faith bears fruit in repentance and a transformed life.
And if you are already a believer, perhaps today is the day to stop treating prayer as a last resort.
Jesus prayed.
The sinless Son, living a genuinely human life, prayed.
How much more should we, who are weak and dependent upon grace, seek the Father through Him?
Pray when you are grateful.
Pray when you are confused.
Pray when you are tempted.
Pray when you have fallen and need to repent.
Pray when you are afraid.
Pray when you have no impressive words left.
Prayer does not make God aware of something He previously overlooked.
It is one of the gracious ways He draws His children into fellowship with Himself.
And you do not have to pretend to be stronger than you are.
God already knows.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
Not to test your theology.
Not to judge your spiritual maturity.
But because the truth about Jesus deserves more than a passing reaction.
Has this helped you understand why Jesus prayed to the Father, or is there still a question you have been afraid to ask?
If you have been wrestling with doubt, you can write, “Lord, help my unbelief.”
And if this teaching has strengthened your faith, share what Scripture helped you understand.
Your testimony might encourage someone who has been silently asking the same question for years.
You never know who is reading the comments while searching for hope.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Not because sharing a post earns God's approval.
But because someone among your family, friends, coworkers, or acquaintances may be struggling with this very question.
Someone may have heard that the prayers of Jesus disprove His deity.
Someone may be close to abandoning faith because nobody has patiently opened the Scriptures with them.
Someone may be carrying shame and desperately need to hear that forgiveness is found in Christ.
And if someone you love is not yet following Jesus, consider sharing this with a personal message rather than turning their spiritual journey into a public spectacle.
Return to it when questions arise.
Read the passages again.
Examine the Greek words in their context.
And allow the Scriptures to deepen your understanding rather than relying on a single sentence pulled away from its chapter.
We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are welcomed, Scripture is handled responsibly, repentance is taken seriously, and the grace of Jesus Christ remains central.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk with us.
These resources are meant to help you study, reflect, pray, and mature in faith.
But creating and sharing biblical content, maintaining resources, and expanding Gospel-centered outreach also require ongoing support.
It is a practical way to partner with a ministry seeking to proclaim Christ, encourage believers, answer difficult questions, and make discipleship resources more accessible.
And there is an important distinction we want to honor.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
God's grace is not for sale.
The Gospel is not a product.
But when believers freely support sound biblical teaching and Gospel outreach, their generosity can become a meaningful expression of love and stewardship.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite others into thoughtful conversations about Christ.
Encourage someone to open the Bible.
Support your local church.
Help a struggling neighbor.
Live the Gospel you profess.
It is the calling of an entire life surrendered to Jesus.
And now, before you leave, remember the scene where we began.
Jesus lifting His eyes toward heaven.
The cross approaching.
The Father hearing the Son.
The eternal glory of Christ revealed through words spoken in the shadow of suffering.
The prayer was not proof that Jesus was less than God.
It was part of the revelation of who He is.
The eternal Son.
The incarnate Savior.
The obedient servant.
The risen Lord.
The One who came from glory, entered our broken world, bore our sins, conquered death, and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
So the next time someone asks, “If Jesus is God, why did He pray?” remember this:
He prayed because He is the Son, not the Father.
He prayed because He truly became human.
He prayed in perfect communion with the Father as He fulfilled the mission of redemption.
And His prayers invite us to behold not a contradiction, but the majesty of the incarnate Christ.
Do not let the mystery drive you away from Him.
Let the truth draw you nearer.
Because the most important question is no longer simply whether you understand why Jesus prayed.
It is whether you have placed your trust in the Jesus who prayed, suffered, died, and rose again to save sinners.
The One who lifted His eyes toward heaven before the cross is the same Savior who can lift a repentant sinner out of shame and into the grace of God.
